comments.author: Baphaddon
comments.body: Made a map tool as well; something I recently thought of and tested to interesting effect; have something generate a top down map, use one of the many image editors to strip it of trees, rocks, foliage and drain all rivers and bodies of water, then feed that into a depth map generator and use that depth map as a height map and immediately you have reasonably sculpted terrain. Then sculpt that terrain as necessary.

comments.body: I started coding a strategy game in ThreeJS, but as the game gets larger, the JS code is getting too complex. Now I'm trying to migrate to Unity. Is ThreeJS appropriate for large projects?

replies.author: NuclearStudent
replies.body:
...what are you doing that Unity would be simpler than ThreeJS?

  
I'm perfectly happy with ThreeJS for my project, but that's because I know exactly the bounds of what I need. I don't need the rendering tools of Unity, nor do I plan to build for console support, or other Unity features. I am making, essentially, a very elaborate spreadsheet, and the visual elements I need that can't be vibecoded easily, I know how to make by hand.

replies.author: sebesbal
replies.body:
It's a game like Sid Meier's Civilization or Railroad Tycoon 3.

Three.js is not a game framework, just a rendering library. A lot of things have to be implemented from scratch. For example, I asked Codex to change the code so I could move a unit on the map with a right mouse click instead of a left click. It managed to do it only on the third try, and when I checked the code, I saw that it had become quite complex. In a normal game framework, this should be a one-line change.

I'm also not a big fan of JavaScript. C# looks much better for large projects.

At this point, I don't really care much about the rendering pipeline and things like that.

replies.author: NuclearStudent
replies.body:
\>  For example, I asked Codex to change the code so I could move a unit on the map with a right mouse click instead of a left click. 

That sounds like a code architecture problem and not a framework problem. I have every action and gesture mapped to a .json that can be easily changed - I didn't even have to manually code this, vibeslop got it out quickly and accurately. It's true that you need to implement your own architecture and engine, but the point of vibecoding is that this is significantly easier.

  
I have a C# backend and a three.JS frontend for my project, but yeah, perfectly valid to work with C# and pure cshtml instead if you prefer.

comments.author: LastJoker96
comments.body:
Disclaimer: This comment is Not related to your specific project, it's mostly related  to the title! 

To be fair, the real question is how could you think that Three.js+AI could even be comparable to a skilled dev using Unity or UE...
It just does not stand a chance at the moment... If you want to play a little and learn some basics, then it's ok...But if you want to learn gamedev for real (FYI learning means no AI Slop or "Vibecoding" ) then pick Unity or UE.
Lemme tell you, vibecoding means nothing, it's the translation of :"I would like to have a skill i don't want to invest time into/i'm unable to achieve"...Useless to say results are never close to being good, especially with gamedev.
Download Unity, follow the tutorial pathway they suggest, then keep grinding C# and software architecture first, then VFX,Sounds,3D Models... The more you "VibeCode", the more time you are wasting without getting real skills.
